title: Beyond Good and Evil
idea: Every philosophy as a hidden confession. Nietzsche asks what each value is for, and whom it serves.
alt: Painting: Beyond Good and Evil as one alpine landscape at dusk. A toppled marble bust, a misty chasm, a rose-lit summit above a lake, and a white mask with ultramarine ribbons.

chapters.name: The prejudices of philosophers
chapters.label: Part 1
chapters.note: Every great philosophy, Nietzsche suspects, is a confession of its author: a defence of a prejudice, dressed up as a proof.

chapters.name: The free spirit
chapters.label: Part 2
chapters.note: Whatever is deep wears a mask. The free spirit keeps its distance, its secrets and its laughter.

chapters.name: Epigrams and interludes
chapters.label: Part 4
chapters.note: Aphorisms, among them the famous warning: gaze long into an abyss, and the abyss gazes back into you.

chapters.name: What is noble?
chapters.label: Part 9
chapters.note: Nobility as a rank of the soul: the reverence a person has for themselves, and the distance they keep from the crowd.

title: Twilight of the Idols
idea: Nietzsche's philosophy in miniature, written in about a week: idols sounded out with a hammer and found hollow.
alt: Painting: a blazing noon. Hollow stone idols with a hammer, a clay cup beside a sprig of hemlock, a sundial with almost no shadow, and a vine-grown temple with an ivy staff tied with an ultramarine ribbon.

chapters.name: Foreword
chapters.note: Sounding out idols with a hammer, as with a tuning fork: the hollow ones give themselves away.

chapters.name: The problem of Socrates
chapters.note: The wisest of every age judged life worthless, and Socrates, dying, called it a sickness. Nietzsche asks what that verdict says about the judges.

chapters.name: How the true world became a fable
chapters.note: The history of an error in six short steps, ending at noon, the moment of the shortest shadow.

chapters.name: What I owe to the ancients
chapters.note: Not the Greeks of the philosophers but of Thucydides and Dionysus: realism, and a yes to life.

title: Essays and Aphorisms
idea: The readable Schopenhauer. Life swings between want and boredom, and the short essays on reading, thinking and noise show how to live with it.
alt: Painting: a winter dusk. An hourglass on ultramarine silk, a storm-bent tree on a hill, porcupines huddled in the snow, and the lamplit window of a study.

chapters.name: On the suffering of the world
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Pain is the positive thing in life, Schopenhauer argues, and happiness only its brief absence.

chapters.name: On the vanity of existence
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Time takes everything we hold. The present keeps slipping into the past, which is why nothing in life quite satisfies.

chapters.name: On thinking for oneself
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Reading is thinking with someone else's head. A little you have thought through beats a library you have only read.

chapters.name: Similes, parables and fables
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: The porcupines on a cold day: they huddle for warmth, prick each other, and settle at a polite distance.

title: Letters from a Stoic
idea: Letters to a friend on how to live: time, reading, crowds, fear and friendship, from a statesman who knew power from the inside.
alt: Painting: a villa terrace above the Bay of Naples. A bronze water clock, a few scrolls on ultramarine cloth, an amphitheatre in a haze of dust, and a ship leaving harbour.

chapters.name: On saving time
chapters.label: Letter 1
chapters.note: Hold every hour in your grasp. Of all we have, only time is truly ours, and we let it slip away.

chapters.name: On reading
chapters.label: Letter 2
chapters.note: Stay with a few great writers and digest them. To be everywhere is to be nowhere.

chapters.name: On crowds
chapters.label: Letter 7
chapters.note: Avoid the crowd. Seneca comes home from the midday games more cruel and less human for having watched.

chapters.name: On travel
chapters.label: Letter 28
chapters.note: Travel cures nothing, because you take yourself along. You need a change of soul, not of sky.

title: Republic
idea: What justice is, worked out by building a city in words. And the cave: prisoners who take the shadows on the wall for the world.
alt: Painting: the Republic as one landscape. A firelit cave with shadows on its wall, a ship in the bay, a pillar of rainbow light in the sky, and a gold ring on ultramarine silk.

chapters.name: The ring of Gyges
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible. Would anyone stay just if no one could see?

chapters.name: The ship of state
chapters.label: Book VI
chapters.note: Sailors fight over the helm and mock the one who studies the stars and the winds. Who should steer a city?

chapters.name: The cave
chapters.label: Book VII
chapters.note: Prisoners take the shadows on the wall for the world. One is led up into the sun, and comes back to be laughed at.

chapters.name: The myth of Er
chapters.label: Book X
chapters.note: A soldier comes back from death and tells how souls choose their next lives beneath a pillar of light, like a rainbow.

title: The Nicomachean Ethics
idea: Virtue as a habit rather than a rule: the mean between too much and too little, found by practice and judgement.
alt: Painting: an Aegean morning. An archery target with an arrow in its centre, a level brass balance, two cups on a table under a pergola, and an armillary sphere on a hill.

chapters.name: The good
chapters.label: Book I
chapters.note: Every action aims at some good. The highest is living well, and like archers we do better with a target to aim at.

chapters.name: The mean
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: Virtue is a habit of choosing the mean between too much and too little, found by practice, not by rule.

chapters.name: Friendship
chapters.label: Book VIII
chapters.note: Friends of use and pleasure come and go. Friends who love each other for who they are wish each other good for its own sake.

chapters.name: Contemplation
chapters.label: Book X
chapters.note: The happiest life is the life of the mind: contemplation, the most self-sufficient thing we do.

title: The Odyssey
idea: Ten years to get home: a man of many turns, a household holding out for him, and the long road back to who he was.
alt: Painting: an Aegean morning. A boulder across a cave mouth with sheep grazing, a small rocky island in the surf, a bow beside a row of twelve axe-heads, and a bed built around an olive tree.

chapters.name: The Cyclops
chapters.label: Book IX
chapters.note: Trapped in the Cyclops' cave behind a boulder, Odysseus calls himself Nobody, blinds the giant and escapes beneath the sheep.

chapters.name: The Sirens
chapters.label: Book XII
chapters.note: Odysseus has himself bound to the mast to hear the Sirens sing, while his crew row on with wax in their ears.

chapters.name: The bow and the axes
chapters.label: Book XXI
chapters.note: Penelope's test: string Odysseus's bow and shoot through twelve axe-heads. Only the beggar in the hall can.

chapters.name: The olive-tree bed
chapters.label: Book XXIII
chapters.note: Penelope's last test: their bed cannot be moved, because Odysseus built it around a living olive tree.

title: The Aeneid
idea: The founding poem of Rome: a refugee from burning Troy carries his father and his gods to a new country, at great cost.
alt: Painting: a city burning across the sea with a wooden horse before it, a new harbour city under scaffolding, a golden bough above a dark cave, and huts on a green hill by a river.

chapters.name: Carthage rising
chapters.label: Book I
chapters.note: Shipwrecked, Aeneas watches the Carthaginians building their city and envies them: their walls are already rising.

chapters.name: The fall of Troy
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: The wooden horse, the night attack, the city in flames: Aeneas tells Dido how Troy fell.

chapters.name: The golden bough
chapters.label: Book VI
chapters.note: To enter the underworld and meet his father, Aeneas must first break a golden bough from a dark tree.

chapters.name: The site of Rome
chapters.label: Book VIII
chapters.note: Aeneas walks with King Evander over the hills where Rome will stand, still a place of huts and cattle.

title: The Three Theban Plays
idea: Oedipus answers the Sphinx and still cannot see himself. Antigone sets the city’s law against an older one.
alt: Painting: Thebes at evening. A burial mound outside the city walls, a winged sphinx above a plain where three roads meet, and a sacred grove of olive and laurel.

chapters.name: Antigone
chapters.note: Antigone buries her brother against the king's decree, setting the city's law against an older, unwritten one.

chapters.name: Oedipus the King
chapters.note: Oedipus solved the Sphinx's riddle. Now he hunts a killer back to the place where three roads meet, and finds himself.

chapters.name: Oedipus at Colonus
chapters.note: Old, blind and exiled, Oedipus reaches the sacred grove at Colonus, near Athens, where at last he is taken in.

title: Parallel Lives
idea: Paired lives of Greeks and Romans, written to show character in small things: a jest, a gesture, a single decision.

cover.alt: Cover of Makers of Rome, a Penguin Classics selection of Plutarch's Lives

alt: Painting: a temple on a citadel wrapped in scaffolding, a yoke tied with a great knot, a river bridge with an eagle standard, and fresh figs on ultramarine cloth.

chapters.name: Pericles
chapters.note: Pericles turns Athens into a building site, and Plutarch marvels that work done so quickly has lasted so long.

chapters.name: Alexander
chapters.note: At Gordium, Alexander is shown a knot no one can untie, and undoes it his own way.

chapters.name: Cato the Elder
chapters.note: Cato drops fresh figs from Carthage in the Senate, grown three days' sail from Rome. Carthage, he says, must be destroyed.

chapters.name: Caesar
chapters.note: Caesar halts at the Rubicon and weighs the cost for a long while, then says, ‘Let the die be cast’, and crosses.

title: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
idea: Thirteen centuries of how a vast, working system comes apart: slowly, from within, in famously measured prose.
alt: Painting: Rome's history in one view. A golden forum, smoke rising beyond the walls, a domed city across a strait, and a fallen column among ruins.

chapters.name: The age of the Antonines
chapters.label: Chapters 1–3
chapters.note: The empire at its height in the second century: peace, law and prosperity, the happiest age, Gibbon thought, in human history.

chapters.name: Constantinople founded
chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.note: Constantine builds a new capital on the Bosphorus, and the empire's centre of gravity moves east.

chapters.name: Alaric sacks Rome
chapters.label: Chapter 31
chapters.note: In 410 the Goths under Alaric enter Rome, the first time in eight centuries the city has fallen to a foreign enemy.

chapters.name: The ruins of Rome
chapters.label: Chapter 71
chapters.note: The last chapter: Rome in the fifteenth century, its monuments quarried and overgrown, seen from the Capitol.

title: Electric Circuits
by: James W. Nilsson & Susan A. Riedel · 10th ed.
idea: The standard first course in circuits: Kirchhoff's laws and a handful of analysis methods, carried from resistors through capacitors and inductors to AC.
alt: Painting: a candlelit study with a wiring board and galvanometer, a row of Leyden jars with a spark, a copper coil on an iron ring beside a compass, and a hand-cranked dynamo.

chapters.name: Techniques of circuit analysis
chapters.note: Kirchhoff's laws: the currents into a node sum to zero, and so do the voltages around a loop. Every analysis method starts there.

chapters.name: Capacitance
chapters.note: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field. The Leyden jar, from 1745, was the first.

chapters.name: Inductance
chapters.note: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field. Faraday's iron ring of 1831 showed that a changing current induces another.

chapters.name: Sinusoidal steady state
chapters.note: Drive a circuit with a sinusoid, as a dynamo does, and phasors turn its differential equations into algebra.

title: Microelectronic Circuits
by: Adel S. Sedra & Kenneth C. Smith · 7th ed.
idea: How semiconductor devices become amplifiers: diodes, MOSFETs and BJTs, their small-signal models, and the circuits built from them.
alt: Painting: an instrument maker's bench with a galena crystal and cat's-whisker wire, a glowing glass valve, a brass speaking trumpet beside a tuning fork, and graduated glass bowls of water.

chapters.name: Signals and amplifiers
chapters.note: An amplifier makes a weak signal stronger without changing its shape: the tuning fork's note, made louder.

chapters.name: Diodes
chapters.note: A diode lets current through one way only. The first were crystal detectors: a fine wire touching a crystal of galena.

chapters.name: Transistors
chapters.note: A small signal at the input controls a large current at the output. The triode valve did it before the transistor.

chapters.name: Frequency response
chapters.note: Every amplifier favours some frequencies over others, as each glass rings at its own pitch.

title: Digital Design
by: M. Morris Mano & Michael D. Ciletti · 6th ed.
idea: From binary numbers and Boolean algebra to gates, flip-flops, registers and memory, with a hardware description language alongside.
alt: Painting: a mechanician's room with a row of brass knife switches, a calculating machine with stepped drums, an open clock movement with its escapement, and a chain of punched loom cards.

chapters.name: Binary numbers
chapters.note: Two states, on and off, are enough to write any number in binary.

chapters.name: Combinational logic
chapters.note: Circuits whose outputs depend only on their present inputs, like adders. Leibniz's stepped drum did addition in brass.

chapters.name: Synchronous sequential logic
chapters.note: Add memory and a clock, and a circuit steps from state to state one tick at a time, like an escapement.

chapters.name: Registers and memory
chapters.note: Rows of stored bits. Jacquard's loom of the early 1800s kept its patterns on punched cards.

title: Digital Integrated Circuits
by: Jan M. Rabaey, Anantha Chandrakasan & Borivoje Nikolić · 2nd ed.
idea: Digital design at the level of the chip: how CMOS is made, how wires and timing limit it, and how gates, arithmetic and memory are built.

cover.alt: Cover of Digital Integrated Circuits, 2nd edition

alt: Painting: a crystal-maker's workshop with a lens projecting light through a pierced stencil onto a shimmering disc, spools of fine gold wire, a chronometer and metronome, and a tray of marbles in a grid, a furnace glowing behind.

chapters.name: The manufacturing process
chapters.note: Chips are printed with light: a pattern is projected through a mask onto silicon, layer by layer.

chapters.name: The wire
chapters.note: At small scales wires stop being ideal; their resistance and capacitance slow every signal down.

chapters.name: Timing issues
chapters.note: A synchronous chip runs on one clock, and keeping its tick aligned across the whole die is a discipline of its own.

chapters.name: Memory and array structures
chapters.note: Memory is a dense grid of cells, each holding one bit, read and written by rows and columns.

title: The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors
idea: Inside the microcontroller cores in most embedded devices: the instruction set, the memory map, interrupts and low-power modes.

cover.alt: Cover of The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors, 3rd edition

alt: Painting: a great house's service passage with a board of servants' bells on springs, an open music box, a tall cabinet of small drawers, and a shuttered lantern on a chair.

chapters.name: The instruction set
chapters.note: A program is a sequence of instructions read in order, like the pins on a music box's cylinder.

chapters.name: The memory system
chapters.note: One address space holds code, data and peripherals, each register in its own drawer.

chapters.name: Exceptions and interrupts
chapters.note: Peripherals ring for the processor's attention, and the interrupt controller decides which bell is answered first.

chapters.name: Low-power features
chapters.note: Sleep modes turn the clock down to a glimmer until an interrupt wakes the core.

title: Elements of Electromagnetics
idea: Vector calculus put to work: static electric and magnetic fields, Maxwell's equations, and waves travelling through space and along lines.

cover.alt: Cover of Elements of Electromagnetics, 6th edition

alt: Painting: a lecture room with an electrostatic machine throwing a spark, iron filings around a bar magnet, ripples spreading in a copper basin, and telegraph wires outside the window.

chapters.name: Electrostatics
chapters.note: Charges at rest and the fields around them, studied with machines like this one since the 1700s.

chapters.name: Magnetostatics
chapters.note: Steady currents and magnets make magnetic fields; iron filings trace their lines.

chapters.name: Electromagnetic waves
chapters.note: Maxwell's equations predict fields that travel as waves, spreading out like ripples on water.

chapters.name: Transmission lines
chapters.note: Two parallel conductors guide a wave from one end to the other, as telegraph wires did.

title: Signals and Systems
by: Alan V. Oppenheim & Alan S. Willsky · 2nd ed.
idea: The language of signals and linear time-invariant systems: convolution, the Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms, and sampling.

cover.alt: Cover of Signals and Systems, 2nd edition

alt: Painting: a music room turned laboratory with a monochord, a bronze bell in a frame, a prism splitting a beam of moonlight into a rainbow, and a slotted disc in front of a spoked wheel.

chapters.name: Signals
chapters.note: A signal is a quantity that varies in time, like the vibration of a plucked string.

chapters.name: Linear time-invariant systems
chapters.note: Strike it once and its ring is the impulse response; for an LTI system, that ring tells you everything.

chapters.name: Fourier series
chapters.note: A periodic signal is a sum of sinusoids, just as a prism splits white light into colours.

chapters.name: Sampling
chapters.note: Look at a signal only at instants and you can still recover it, if you look fast enough. Too slow, and a wheel seems to turn backwards.

title: Digital Signal Processing
by: John G. Proakis & Dimitris G. Manolakis · 4th ed.
idea: Processing sampled signals with computers: the z-transform, the DFT and its fast algorithms, and the design of digital filters.

cover.alt: Cover of Digital Signal Processing, 4th edition

alt: Painting: an acoustics laboratory with brass weights hanging on threads of graduated lengths, a rack of tuning forks, a case of butterflies pinned in an X, and coloured glass panes before a lamp.

chapters.name: Discrete-time signals
chapters.note: A signal known only at evenly spaced instants: a row of values, one per sample.

chapters.name: The discrete Fourier transform
chapters.note: The DFT measures how much of each frequency a finite signal holds, one tuning fork per bin.

chapters.name: The fast Fourier transform
chapters.note: The FFT computes the DFT in N log N steps, built from crossing pairs of operations called butterflies.

chapters.name: Design of digital filters
chapters.note: A filter passes some frequencies and stops others, as coloured glass passes some light.

title: Communication Systems
idea: How information crosses a noisy channel: random processes, analogue and pulse modulation, digital transmission and Shannon's limits.
alt: Painting: a coastal signal station at night with a telegraph key and paper tape, a lighthouse beam sweeping the sea outside, a conch shell, and a great coil of submarine cable.

chapters.name: Random processes
chapters.note: Every signal is judged against noise, modelled as a random process: the sea you hear in a shell.

chapters.name: Continuous-wave modulation
chapters.note: A message rides on a carrier by varying its amplitude or frequency, as a lighthouse signals by changing its light.

chapters.name: Pulse modulation
chapters.note: A signal sent as a train of pulses, the idea behind the telegraph and every digital link since.

chapters.name: Information theory
chapters.note: Every channel has a capacity, Shannon showed, and below it a message can get through almost without error.

title: Modern Control Engineering
idea: Making systems behave through feedback: transfer functions, transient response, stability, root locus, frequency response and state space.

cover.alt: Cover of Modern Control Engineering, 5th edition

alt: Painting: a ship's cabin by lamplight with a steam engine and flyball governor, a gimballed compass, a ball in a bowl and a ball balanced on an upturned bowl, and the ship's wheel through the doorway.

chapters.name: Feedback control
chapters.note: Watt's governor senses an engine's speed and closes the steam valve as it rises: the classic feedback loop.

chapters.name: Transient response
chapters.note: Disturb a system and watch it settle, like a compass needle swinging back to north.

chapters.name: Stability
chapters.note: A ball in a bowl returns when nudged; a ball on top of one runs away. Stability is telling the two apart.

chapters.name: PID control
chapters.note: Proportional, integral and derivative action, first worked out for steering ships.

title: University Physics
by: Hugh D. Young & Roger A. Freedman · 14th ed.
idea: Calculus-based physics from the ground up: motion, forces, energy, rotation, gravitation, waves and heat.
alt: Painting: a lecture room with a ball at the top of an inclined plane hung with bells, a gyroscope, a brass orrery around a lamp, and Hero's steam sphere spinning over a flame.

chapters.name: Newton's laws of motion
chapters.note: Galileo timed balls rolling down a slope; Newton's three laws explain what he saw.

chapters.name: Rotation
chapters.note: A spinning body has angular momentum, which is why a gyroscope holds its axis.

chapters.name: Gravitation
chapters.note: One law of attraction keeps every planet on its orbit, the motion an orrery shows in brass.

chapters.name: Thermodynamics
chapters.note: Heat is energy that can do work, as Hero of Alexandria's steam sphere showed two thousand years ago.

title: Linear Algebra and Its Applications
idea: Linear algebra as a working tool: elimination, vector spaces, orthogonality, determinants and eigenvalues, with applications throughout.

cover.alt: Cover of Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 4th edition

alt: Painting: a cartographer's study with a sea chart, compass rose and dividers, a pantograph copying a vase, sand forming a star pattern on a bowed brass plate, and a thread stretched between scattered pins.

chapters.name: Vector spaces
chapters.note: Vectors have size and direction, like a course plotted on a chart, and can be added and scaled.

chapters.name: Linear transformations
chapters.note: A pantograph copies a drawing at a new scale: one linear map applied to every point at once.

chapters.name: Orthogonality and least squares
chapters.note: The line that best fits scattered points, the method Gauss used to find a lost planet in 1801.

chapters.name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
chapters.note: Bow a plate and the sand gathers on the lines that stay still; each pattern is an eigenmode.

title: Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
idea: The mathematics of computing: logic and proof, number theory, induction, counting, and graphs and trees.

cover.alt: Cover of Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 8th edition

alt: Painting: a library at night with a row of toppling dominoes, a model town of seven bridges, a cipher made of stacked wooden discs, and strings of coloured beads.

chapters.name: Number theory and cryptography
chapters.note: Arithmetic that wraps around, like the discs of a cipher wheel. Modular arithmetic is what modern cryptography is built on.

chapters.name: Induction
chapters.note: Show the first domino falls and that each one knocks over the next, and they all fall.

chapters.name: Counting
chapters.note: How many necklaces can these beads make? Counting arguments answer without listing them all.

chapters.name: Graphs
chapters.note: Could you cross each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once? Euler proved in 1736 that you could not, and graph theory began.

title: Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems
by: William E. Boyce & Richard C. DiPrima · 10th ed.
idea: Equations of change: first- and second-order equations, systems, Laplace transforms, and the classic equations of heat and waves.

cover.alt: Cover of Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems, 10th edition

alt: Painting: a country-house laboratory with a steaming cup of tea and a thermometer, a weight on a coiled spring, hares and a fox in the moonlit meadow outside, and wax melting along rods heated by a candle.

chapters.name: First-order equations
chapters.note: A cup of tea cools by Newton's law of cooling, a first-order equation.

chapters.name: Second-order linear equations
chapters.note: A weight on a spring oscillates; its motion is the textbook second-order equation.

chapters.name: Systems of equations
chapters.note: Hares and foxes rise and fall in turn, described by a pair of coupled equations.

chapters.name: The heat equation
chapters.note: Heat spreads along a rod by a partial differential equation, melting the wax nearest the flame first.

title: Probability and Random Processes for Electrical Engineering
idea: Probability built for engineers: random variables, limit theorems, estimation and random processes.

cover.alt: Cover of Probability and Random Processes for Electrical Engineering, 2nd edition

alt: Painting: a study at night with dice and cards on a baize table, a Galton board of pins with balls piling into a bell curve, a microscope by a candle, and a sextant by a window onto the sea.

chapters.name: Probability
chapters.note: Probability began with games of chance and a question about dice.

chapters.name: The central limit theorem
chapters.note: Add up enough random bounces and a bell curve appears, as Galton's board shows.

chapters.name: Random processes
chapters.note: Pollen in water jiggles at random, Brown saw in 1827: a random process unfolding in time.

chapters.name: Estimation
chapters.note: Estimating an unknown from noisy measurements, as a navigator fixes a position from star sights.
